extracted.intended_audience: agency rulewriters, administrative-law attorneys, regulatory stakeholders, and public commenters working on notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for agency rulemaking and public comments focused on statutory interpretation (especially post-Loper Bright) and the legal foundations for proposed or existing regulations. Useful for analyzing whether rules rest on legally defensible readings of statutes, procedural requirements, and doctrines such as Chevron, Skidmore, and the major-questions doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to the single best reading of the statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must adhere to the single best reading of the statutes they administer (courts require agencies to adopt the best reading of a statute rather than any permissible alternative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple excerpts cite Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (144 S. Ct. / 603 U.S. 369 (2024)) emphasizing that courts look to the best reading of a statute: “it makes no sense to speak of a ‘permissible’ interpretation . . . that is not the one the court, after applying all relevant interpretive tools, concludes is best.” Agencies should analyze statutory text and show that their interpretation is the best reading, not merely reasonable or permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference is no longer a basis for upholding agency interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron deference was overruled by Loper Bright; agencies cannot rely on Chevron as legal support for their statutory interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents repeatedly note that Loper Bright overruled Chevron and that agencies and commenters must treat prior reliance on Chevron as no longer controlling. Rule writers should not invoke Chevron as a backstop; instead they must justify interpretations under the best-reading standard and other appropriate doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the major questions doctrine where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should assess whether a rule implicates the major questions doctrine (i.e., whether the action addresses questions of vast economic or political significance requiring clear congressional authorization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several agency notices analyze whether the major questions doctrine corroborates or independently supports their conclusions about statutory authority. When a rule addresses a major question, agencies should explain why the statute authorizes the action and cannot rely on broad or ambiguous readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress can still provide a ‘degree of deference’ via clear delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: Loper Bright did not eliminate Congress's ability to delegate discretionary authority; where Congress clearly delegates, agencies may be afforded a degree of deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pages note that the Court acknowledged Congress may 'delegate . . . discretionary authority to any agency' and such delegations can sustain agency discretion. Rule writers should identify and explain any statutory delegations relied upon to show why agency interpretation merits weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Skidmore and other pre-Chevron frameworks where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: With Chevron abrogated, courts and agencies may rely on the Skidmore framework (and other interpretive tools) to evaluate the persuasive force of agency interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and reviewers should articulate the bases for Skidmore-type weight (e.g., consistency, thoroughness, expertise, persuasive reasoning). Several documents state that agency rules are again reviewed under Skidmore or similar standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish interpretive rules/policy statements from legislative rules (notice-and-comment implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive rules and policy statements generally do not carry the force and effect of law; provisions that were not issued through notice-and-comment rulemaking should not be treated as binding regulatory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Department of Labor proposes to remove parts of the CFR that were not originally issued through notice-and-comment because they are interpretive or policy statements, and to repurpose them as sub-regulatory guidance. Agencies should identify whether a provision is interpretive (and thus nonbinding) or legislative (requiring notice-and-comment) and explain the chosen treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassess prior agency actions that relied on Chevron
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should review and, if necessary, revise or rescind prior rules and interpretations that depended on Chevron deference, ensuring they conform to the best-reading standard or other valid legal bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple Federal Register entries describe agencies revisiting earlier rules (e.g., Endangered Species Act definitions, water quality certifications, FLSA companionship services) because prior judicial or agency reliance on Chevron no longer supplies legal cover. Documentation should explain the reconsideration and the alternative legal grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proposing rescission, provide independent statutory and evidentiary bases
rubrics_metrics.description: If rescinding a prior finding or standard, agencies must present statutory analysis and, where relevant, alternative bases (best reading, scientific record, lack of requisite statutory authority) to justify rescission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA examples show rescission proposals that rely on multiple independent rationales (best reading of statutory terms, major questions analysis, re-evaluation of scientific evidence). Rulemakings that repeal major prior actions should present thorough legal and factual support rather than relying on Chevron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments may and should challenge whether a policy rests on agency interpretation rather than the best statutory reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments can (and in examples did) argue that a policy relies on agency interpretation rather than the best reading of the statute, rendering it legally indefensible under current precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (e.g., CPAC-CRF challenging PECE) show commenters invoking Loper Bright and Executive Orders to argue that policies are legally vulnerable. Commenters should frame arguments around statutory text, canons, precedent, and whether agency action is the best reading of the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that courts decide statutory interpretation under APA §706
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues of statutory interpretation are for courts to decide under APA section 706; agencies should not assume judicial deference to their interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and commenters should draft legal reasoning mindful that courts will independently determine the best reading of the statute when reviewing arbitrary-and-capricious or statutory-interpretation questions under section 706.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply all relevant interpretive tools and precedents to identify the best reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory interpretation must use the full suite of interpretive tools (text, structure, history, canons, precedent) and consider Supreme Court guidance to conclude what the best reading is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loper Bright language quoted on the page instructs that courts apply all relevant tools; agencies should mirror that approach in rule preambles and responses to comments, demonstrating why their interpretation emerges as the best reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain practical effects and stability implications for regulated entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should discuss how interpretive changes (and the end of Chevron) affect regulated entities' ability to plan and the stability of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some documents note that Chevron produced instability and that its abrogation reduces agency ability to change policy unilaterally; agencies should explain effects on regulated parties and how the new interpretation promotes predictability or identifies transitional measures.
